## Proof

**Answer:** $p$ must be an involution whose transpositions form a **non-crossing matching** (equivalently, a $231$-avoiding involution).

---

### Setup

An involution is a permutation $p$ with $p = p^{-1}$, so its cycle decomposition consists only of fixed points and transpositions. A *pattern* of $p$ is any permutation obtained by deleting some entries from the one-line notation of $p$ and standardizing (relabeling to $\{1,\dots,k\}$ preserving order).

A permutation fails to be an involution iff it has a cycle of length $\geq 3$. The smallest such patterns are the two $3$-cycles $231 = (1\;2\;3)$ and $312 = (1\;3\;2)$.

### Crossing transpositions force a $231$ pattern

Suppose $p$ has two transpositions $(a\;b)$ and $(c\;d)$ with $a < c < b < d$ (the transpositions **cross**). In one-line notation:
$$p(a) = b,\quad p(c) = d,\quad p(b) = a.$$
Consider the subsequence at positions $a, c, b$ (in this order): the values are $b, d, a$. Since $a < b < d$, standardizing gives $2, 3, 1 = \mathbf{231}$, which is a $3$-cycle and **not** an involution. (The case $c < a < d < b$ is identical by symmetry.)

**Conclusion:** If $p$ has any pair of crossing transpositions, then $p$ contains a non-involution pattern, violating the hypothesis.

### Non-crossing involutions have only involution patterns

Now suppose $p$ is an involution whose transpositions form a **non-crossing matching** (no two transpositions $(a\;b)$, $(c\;d)$ satisfy $a < c < b < d$), with all other elements fixed.

**Claim:** Deleting any single entry from $p$ yields another non-crossing involution.

- If we delete a **fixed point** $i$: the remaining matching is unchanged and still non-crossing; the result is still an involution. ✓
- If we delete an element $i$ belonging to a transposition $(i\;j)$: the partner $j$ becomes a fixed point, and all other transpositions are untouched. Removing one pair from a non-crossing matching leaves a non-crossing matching. After relabeling (which preserves relative order of all remaining endpoints), the matching remains non-crossing, and the permutation remains an involution. ✓

By induction on the number of deletions, **every** pattern of $p$ is a non-crossing involution, hence an involution.

### Equivalence with $231$-avoidance

Since $p = p^{-1}$, the set of patterns of $p$ equals the set of patterns of $p^{-1} = p$. The inverse of $231$ is $312$, so $p$ contains $231$ iff $p$ contains $312$. We showed crossing $\Leftrightarrow$ contains $231$, so:

$$p \text{ has all patterns involutions} \iff p \text{ has non-crossing transpositions} \iff p \text{ avoids } 231\;(\text{and } 312).$$

### Conclusion

$p$ must be an involution whose transpositions form a non-crossing matching on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ (with all other elements fixed), equivalently a $231$-avoiding (or $312$-avoiding) involution.

### PROOF COMPLETE

An involution is a permutation $p$ with $p = p^{-1}$, so its cycle decomposition consists only of fixed points and transpositions. A permutation fails to be an involution iff it has a cycle of length $\geq 3$. The smallest such patterns are the two $3$-cycles $231 = (1\;2\;3)$ and $312 = (1\;3\;2)$.

### Crossing transpositions force a $231$ pattern

Suppose $p$ has two transpositions $(a\;b)$ and $(c\;d)$ with $a < c < b < d$ (the transpositions **cross**). In one-line notation:
$$p(a) = b,\quad p(c) = d,\quad p(b) = a.$$
Consider the subsequence at positions $a, c, b$ (in this order): the values are $b, d, a$. Since $a < b < d$, standardizing gives $2, 3, 1 = \mathbf{231}$, which is a $3$-cycle and **not** an involution. (The case $c < a < d < b$ is identical by symmetry.)

**Conclusion:** If $p$ has any pair of crossing transpositions, then $p$ contains a non-involution pattern, violating the hypothesis.

### Non-crossing involutions have only involution patterns

Now suppose $p$ is an involution whose transpositions form a **non-crossing matching** (no two transpositions $(a\;b)$, $(c\;d)$ satisfy $a < c < b < d$), with all other elements fixed.

**Claim:** Deleting any single entry from $p$ yields another non-crossing involution.

- If we delete a **fixed point** $i$: the remaining matching is unchanged and still non-crossing; the result is still an involution. ✓
- If we delete an element $i$ belonging to a transposition $(i\;j)$: the partner $j$ becomes a fixed point, and all other transpositions are untouched. Removing one pair from a non-crossing matching leaves a non-crossing matching. After relabeling (which preserves relative order of all remaining endpoints), the matching remains non-crossing, and the permutation remains an involution. ✓

By induction on the number of deletions, **every** pattern of $p$ is a non-crossing involution, hence an involution.

### Equivalence with $231$-avoidance

Since $p = p^{-1}$, the set of patterns of $p$ equals the set of patterns of $p^{-1} = p$. The inverse of $231$ is $312$, so $p$ contains $231$ iff $p$ contains $312$. We showed crossing $\Leftrightarrow$ contains $231$, so:

$$p \text{ has all patterns involutions} \iff p \text{ has non-crossing transpositions} \iff p \text{ avoids } 231\;(\text{and } 312).$$

### Conclusion

$p$ must be an involution whose transpositions form a non-crossing matching on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ (with all other elements fixed), equivalently a $231$-avoiding (or $312$-avoiding) involution.
